title: Three AI Activities You Can Do With Your Family Tonight
subtitle: Hands-on explorations that don't require any tech background
subject: Family Conversations
Digital Literacy
Media Literacy
summary: Three short activities designed for families to do together — no prior knowledge needed. Each one builds real intuition about how AI works and opens conversation naturally, without feeling like homework.

body.text: The best way to understand AI is to use it with a purpose. These activities give your family something concrete to look at and discuss together. They're designed so that you and your child are on equal footing — neither of you needs to be the expert.
Activity 1: The Same Question, Three Ways (20 min)

Pick a question your family genuinely wants to know the answer to — something local and specific works best, like 'What's a good hiking trail near us?' or 'How does our city's water get treated?' Then find the answer three ways: a regular web search, an AI chatbot, and by asking someone who actually knows (a neighbor, a teacher, a quick call). Compare what you got.

items: Did any of the three sources contradict each other?
Which answer felt most trustworthy, and why?
Did the AI answer sound confident even where it was vague or wrong?
Which source would you use again for this kind of question?

body.text: This activity builds the habit of verification without making it feel like a lesson. It also surfaces something important: AI often sounds equally confident whether it's right or wrong.

Before anyone opens a device: each person sketches or describes what they imagine when they hear a word — try 'teacher,' 'scientist,' 'programmer,' or 'nurse.' Then use a free AI image generator (Adobe Firefly and Canva AI are both free and appropriate for families) to generate images for those same words. Compare.

items: Does the AI's image look like what you pictured?
Who is in the AI's image? What are they wearing? Where are they?
If the AI showed mostly one type of person, why do you think that is?
Does this change how you think about AI-generated images you've seen before?

body.text: This activity introduces the concept of training data bias in a way that feels immediate and personal rather than abstract. Most families find the comparison genuinely surprising.

Find a recipe your family likes and ask an AI chatbot to rewrite it — in a different style, for a different dietary restriction, or 'for a five-year-old who hates vegetables.' Then actually try to cook one version. This is less about AI and more about noticing: where did the AI do well? Where did it miss something a person would have caught?

items: Did the AI make any substitutions that seemed wrong or odd?
Did it miss anything about your family's actual kitchen — equipment, ingredients you have?
Would you use an AI for recipe help again? For what kind of question?
What would a person — a relative who cooks well, a chef — have done differently?

body.text: Cooking grounds the conversation in something tangible. It also naturally raises the question of what 'context' an AI is missing, which is one of its core limitations.

There's no right answer to any of the discussion questions above. The point is that your family is building a shared vocabulary for talking about AI — which is more useful than any single fact you could learn about it.
